meta.name: Dog-Friendly Hikes in the East Bay (2026)
meta.title_tag: Dog-Friendly Hikes in the East Bay (2026)
meta.excerpt: Ten East Bay trail destinations where dogs are genuinely welcome — including the region's famous off-leash voice-control rules — with every policy checked against official East Bay Regional Park District pages in July 2026.
meta.meta_description: 10 dog-friendly hikes in the East Bay for 2026 — off-leash Point Isabel, shady Redwood, Mission Peak & more, with rules verified on official EBRPD pages.

hero.alt: Mission Peak Regional Preserve — from Wooffy's Bay Area dog guide (photo: Oleg Alexandrov, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons)

body_html:
The East Bay Regional Park District is one of the few park agencies in the country that lets dogs hike off-leash under voice control on hundreds of miles of trail — but the rules change trail by trail, and a few beloved spots ban dogs outright. This guide covers ten destinations from the Richmond shoreline to the Fremont hills, and every dog policy was checked against its official EBRPD (or US Fish & Wildlife) page and verified July 2026. Hours, fees, and closures change, so treat the linked official page as the final word before you drive out.

Alongside the official rules, we distilled recurring themes from dog-owner reviews across Google, Yelp, Reddit, BringFido, and AllTrails — see the “What dog owners say” notes under each entry (a theme is included only when it shows up on at least two independent platforms).

Quick Picks

CategoryPick

Best shade on a hot dayReinhardt Redwood Regional Park
Best easy lakeside walkLake Chabot Regional Park
Best big-climb workoutMission Peak Regional Preserve (cool mornings only)
Best bay views on paved trailCoyote Hills Regional Park

Point Isabel Regional Shoreline (Richmond)

Address: 2701 Isabel Street, Richmond · Fenced: No · Hours: 5am–10pm unless otherwise posted

★ 4.8 · 2,056 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance~3.5 mi of paths
Elevation gainNegligible (flat)
DifficultyEasy
Off-leashYes, park-wide (voice control)
Leash ruleLeashed in lots and on streets; carry one per dog
ShadeMinimal; open and windy
WaterDrinking taps and an on-site dog wash
Parking / feeFree

Point Isabel is the East Bay's flagship dog outing: 23 flat shoreline acres, plus 20 more at North Point Isabel across the Hoffman Channel, with the Golden Gate Bridge, Marin, and Brooks Island on the horizon. It draws well over a million visitors a year, nearly all with dogs, so this is a social scene rather than a solitary hike. Point Isabel's own rules still apply: carry a six-foot leash for each dog, keep your dog in sight, leash any dog that shows aggression, and bag the waste.

The south-side paths are level, paved or packed gravel, and over four feet wide — easy going for seniors and small dogs; North Point Isabel's are dirt and old asphalt. The point is exposed and often windy, which keeps it cool and usable on warm afternoons when the hill parks bake. Mudpuppy's Tub & Scrub and the Sit & Stay Café sit inside the park, so you can hose off a muddy dog before the drive home — and at low tide the bay margin gets genuinely muddy.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 one of the largest fully off-leash dog parks in the country, with room to roam for miles along the shoreline
  • 👍 on-site dog wash and dog-friendly cafe make post-mud cleanup part of the routine
  • 👍 flat, mostly paved paths with bay and Golden Gate views work for owners and dogs of any age
  • ⚠️ weekends get crowded and can feel chaotic
  • ⚠️ tidal mudflats produce thick, smelly mud and paths turn sloppy in the rainy season
  • ⚠️ unpicked poop and the occasional inattentive owner come up repeatedly

Recurring themes from owner reviews across Yelp, BringFido, TripAdvisor, DogTrekker.

Reinhardt Redwood Regional Park (Oakland)

Address: 7867 Redwood Road, Oakland · Fenced: No · Hours: Main gate roughly 8am–6pm winter to 8am–8pm summer; park curfew 10pm–5am

★ 4.8 · 3,528 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance~5 mi signature loop
Elevation gain~850 ft
DifficultyModerate
Off-leashYes on the upland ridge trails
Leash ruleLeashed on the Stream, Bridle, and Serpentine Prairie trails
ShadeHeavy; cool redwood canyon
WaterTaps at staging areas; keep dogs out of the creek
Parking / fee$5/vehicle, weekends and holidays Apr–Oct, Redwood Gate only

A 1,833-acre coast redwood forest ten minutes over the ridge from Oakland, with nearly 40 miles of trail and the best hot-day shade in this guide — the canyon floor stays cool when the rest of the East Bay is baking. The signature loop pairs the shaded Stream Trail along Redwood Creek with the sunnier West Ridge Trail up top, about five miles with 850 feet of climb.

Mind the split in the rules: the wide, gentle Stream Trail is a posted leash trail, because the creek holds a historic native rainbow trout strain. Legal off-leash time is on the undeveloped ridge trails, and only under genuine voice control. Keep dogs out of the water entirely — the district warns that raw salmon and trout can carry a parasite that is often fatal to dogs. Cell service is patchy in the canyon, so download the map first.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 shaded redwood-canyon trails stay cool even on hot days
  • 👍 off-leash under voice control on most upper trails, with a culture of responsible dog owners
  • 👍 good mix of wide fire roads and quieter single track for different fitness levels
  • ⚠️ the popular flat Stream Trail is leash-required (resource protection area) and off-leash fines are steep, which surprises first-timers
  • ⚠️ poison oak crowds the edges of narrower routes like French Trail
  • ⚠️ weekend parking fills early and the main lot charges per-car plus per-dog fees in season

Recurring themes from owner reviews across AllTrails, Yelp, TripAdvisor, DogTrekker.

Tilden Regional Park (Berkeley)

Address: Entrances off Wildcat Canyon Road and Grizzly Peak Boulevard, Berkeley · Fenced: No · Hours: 5am–10pm unless otherwise posted

★ 4.8 · 3,971 Google reviews · on Google Maps

DistanceFlexible; 2–8 mi
Elevation gainVaries by route
DifficultyEasy–moderate
Off-leashYes in undeveloped open space
Leash ruleLeashed on paved Nimitz Way; no dogs in the Nature Area or at Lake Anza
ShadeMixed; shaded canyons, open ridges
WaterTaps at staging areas; no lake swimming
Parking / feeFree

Tilden's 2,079 acres hold plenty of good dog hiking, but the boundaries matter. The entire 740-acre Tilden Nature Area — Little Farm, Jewel Lake, and the Wildcat Peak trails at the north end — is posted no-dogs and staff enforce it, and the Lake Anza swim beach is off-limits under the district's beach rule. Base yourself in the main park's open space instead: the Inspiration Point staging area on Wildcat Canyon Road is the classic launch, with off-leash fire trails fanning out along the ridge. Paved Nimitz Way from Inspiration Point is a leash-required multi-use path.

Heads-up for 2026: the district is running fuels-reduction work across Tilden from May through December with intermittent road and trail closures, and a stretch of the Wildcat Gorge Trail near Brook Road is closed for creek restoration, with reopening planned by January 2027. Check the official page before you drive out.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 huge trail network where dogs can be off-leash under voice control in undeveloped areas
  • 👍 varied terrain from shaded creek canyons to ridge trails with bay views keeps walks interesting
  • 👍 multiple free trailhead parking lots, unlike many nearby regional parks
  • ⚠️ dogs are banned from the Tilden Nature Area around Jewel Lake and from the Little Farm, and staff enforce it strictly
  • ⚠️ coyote sightings near trails make owners keep dogs close
  • ⚠️ trails stay muddy and slippery for days after rain, and Lake Anza has a history of toxic-algae closures that are dangerous for dogs

Recurring themes from owner reviews across AllTrails, TripAdvisor, Yelp, Hikes Dogs Love.

Sibley Volcanic Regional Preserve (Oakland / Orinda)

Address: Main staging area: 6800 Skyline Blvd, Oakland · Fenced: No · Hours: November–February 7am–6pm; March–October 7am–10pm

★ 4.7 · 1,415 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance~3.5 mi loop (1.7 mi short option)
Elevation gain~550 ft
DifficultyEasy–moderate
Off-leashYes on unposted preserve trails
Leash ruleLeashed on the Skyline National Trail; no dogs on Huckleberry
ShadeLittle; open fire road
WaterFaucets at the staging area
Parking / feeFree

Hike a 10-million-year-old volcano with your dog. Round Top (1,763 feet) anchors a compact network with a self-guided geology tour, quarry overlooks, and the well-known hillside labyrinth; the full Round Top–Volcanic–Skyline loop runs about 3.5 miles, and a 1.7-mile overlook loop covers the highlights. Dogs are welcome across the preserve — but explicitly not on the neighboring Huckleberry Botanic Regional Preserve, whose trails connect straight to Sibley's south end, so watch the signs where the two meet. The Skyline National Trail from the staging area north to the EBMUD boundary is a leash-only stretch.

The Skyline Boulevard lot is small and fills on weekend mornings, when commercial walkers with large packs work the main trails; the Old Tunnel Road staging area on the Orinda side is the quieter way in. Trails are mostly open fire road with patchy shade and seasonal cattle — fine most of the year, warm at midday in summer.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 dependable off-leash voice-control hiking just minutes from Oakland and Berkeley
  • 👍 volcanic terrain and the hilltop labyrinth make even short loops feel memorable
  • 👍 staging area has water faucets handy for filling dog bowls
  • ⚠️ commercial dog walkers with large packs dominate the main trails, and weekends get crowded
  • ⚠️ seasonal cattle grazing means leashing up in some sections, with ticks and poison oak just off-trail
  • ⚠️ small trailhead lots fill quickly

Recurring themes from owner reviews across Yelp, BringFido, TripAdvisor, Hikes Dogs Love.

Briones Regional Park (Martinez / Lafayette)

Address: Alhambra Staging Area: 273-181 Brookwood Dr, Martinez; Bear Creek Staging Area: 1611 Bear Creek Road, Lafayette · Fenced: No · Hours: Roughly 8am–5pm winter to 8am–8pm summer; parking lots 8am to sunset

★ 4.7 · 1,294 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance~7 mi loop (5–8 mi options)
Elevation gain~1,150 ft
DifficultyModerate
Off-leashYes across most of the park
Leash ruleLeashed on posted Alhambra Creek trails and around cattle
ShadeSparse on ridges; oak in the canyons
WaterNone for dogs; troughs are for livestock
Parking / fee$5/vehicle when attended; cash only

Briones is the big, quiet one: 6,255 acres of rolling ridge and oak woodland with a fraction of the crowds of the Oakland hills parks, and spring wildflowers on the grassy tops. A typical loop from the Bear Creek or Alhambra staging areas runs six to eight miles over about 1,150 feet of climb. The leash-required trails are posted and clustered near the Alhambra Creek entrance; beyond them this is classic voice-control country. Cattle graze throughout — the district asks you to leash or heel your dog and walk around herds rather than through them.

Shade is scarce on the ridge tops, so start early in summer and carry all your dog's water; the troughs are for livestock. Winter and spring turn the fire roads to deep, lingering mud. Bring cash for the kiosk.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 vast, comparatively uncrowded open space where most trails allow off-leash dogs
  • 👍 rolling ridge trails deliver big panoramic views toward Mt. Diablo and the bay
  • 👍 options range from mellow valley strolls to leg-burning ridge climbs
  • ⚠️ free-roaming cattle share the trails, so dogs need solid recall or a leash near herds
  • ⚠️ winter and spring mud gets severe and lingers for days after rain
  • ⚠️ largely exposed with little shade, so summer afternoons are brutal

Recurring themes from owner reviews across AllTrails, TripAdvisor, Wag!, Hikes Dogs Love.

Anthony Chabot Regional Park (Castro Valley / Oakland)

Address: 9999 Redwood Road, Castro Valley · Fenced: No · Hours: Park curfew 10pm–5am; campground gates 8am–10pm

★ 4.7 · 1,174 Google reviews · on Google Maps

DistanceFlexible; 3–12 mi
Elevation gainVaries by route
DifficultyEasy–moderate
Off-leashYes on undeveloped trails
Leash ruleLeashed in the campground, staging, and picnic areas
ShadeMixed; eucalyptus groves and grassland
WaterTaps at staging and campground; not Lake Chabot
Parking / feeFree day-use

With 3,304 acres and 70 miles of trail through grassland, chaparral, and eucalyptus, Anthony Chabot is where East Bay dog walkers go for mileage without crowds — from the easy 2.9-mile Grass Valley and Brandon loop to all-day ridge routes. The wide MacDonald and Grass Valley fire roads are dog-walking standards, with the sightlines and passing room to prove it, and the park drops downhill to the Lake Chabot loop if you want water at the turnaround (for looking only — the lake is closed to dogs).

Plan around 2026 work: the Goldenrod Trail between Jackson Grade and Jalquin Trail is closed May 18–November 20 for fuels reduction, Willowview Trail is closed, and a section of Redtail Trail is out from storm damage. Fast mountain-bike traffic shares many of the fire roads, so expect to step aside. Check the official page for the current closure list.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 large trail network with off-leash freedom in undeveloped areas
  • 👍 dog-friendly campground earns consistent praise for cleanliness and upkeep
  • 👍 varied scenery from eucalyptus forest to ridge views and lakeside stretches
  • ⚠️ keep dogs completely out of Lake Chabot - toxic blue-green algae blooms here have killed dogs
  • ⚠️ fast mountain-bike traffic shares many of the fire roads, forcing frequent step-asides
  • ⚠️ some trail sections get overgrown and less maintained

Recurring themes from owner reviews across AllTrails, TripAdvisor, BringFido, The Dyrt.

Lake Chabot Regional Park (Castro Valley)

Address: 17600 Lake Chabot Rd, Castro Valley · Fenced: No · Hours: Gates roughly 6am–6pm winter to 6am–9pm in peak season

★ 4.7 · 4,160 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance3.5 mi paved / ~9 mi full loop
Elevation gainFlat shore; hilly full loop
DifficultyEasy–moderate
Off-leashBackcountry trails only
Leash ruleLeashed on the paved shore, marina, and picnic areas
ShadeMixed; forest and open hillside
WaterTaps at the marina; no lake contact (algae)
Parking / fee$5/vehicle

The 315-acre reservoir offers the easiest scenic miles in this guide: a flat, partly paved shoreline path past fishing piers, a marina café, and restrooms — friendly for puppies, seniors, and small dogs on the leashed West Shore. Push past the pavement onto the East Shore and backcountry trails and it becomes a real hike, up to a nine-mile loop with far fewer people, where voice-control off-leash applies toward Anthony Chabot.

The non-negotiable: keep dogs out of the lake. A blue-green algae Danger advisory was posted as of July 2026, the toxins can be fatal to dogs, and swimming is never permitted here regardless. Check the water-quality banner on the official page before every visit.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 scenic lakeside loop with paved, accessible stretches near the marina that suit older dogs and casual walkers
  • 👍 dog-friendly marina cafe patio is a favorite post-hike stop
  • 👍 long loop options (about 9 miles) move from open hillside to shoreline to shady forest
  • ⚠️ absolutely no water contact for dogs - blue-green algae blooms here have been fatal to dogs
  • ⚠️ paid parking plus a per-dog fee, and lots jam up by late morning on weekends
  • ⚠️ the paved West Shore stretch gets very crowded on weekends

Recurring themes from owner reviews across Yelp, AllTrails, BringFido, TripAdvisor.

Garin & Dry Creek Pioneer Regional Parks (Hayward / Union City)

Address: 1320 Garin Avenue, Hayward · Fenced: No · Hours: Gates roughly 8am–6pm winter to 8am–9pm summer; park curfew 10pm–5am

★ 4.7 · 866 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance~6 mi High Ridge Loop
Elevation gain~1,150 ft
DifficultyModerate
Off-leashYes on the trails (voice control)
Leash ruleLeashed in lots, picnic areas, and lawns; heel around cattle
ShadeSparse; exposed grassland
WaterTaps near the barn; carry your own on the ridge
Parking / fee$5/vehicle when attended; cash only

These two adjoining old-ranch parks cover more than 5,800 acres and 35-plus miles of trail through narrow valleys and open hills, with panoramic Bay views from the ridgelines and a fraction of the Oakland hills' foot traffic. The official page's dog section is unusually clear: voice control at all times, a leash in hand and ready, and specific warnings not to let dogs chase cattle and to watch for coyotes — both are genuinely present here.

The mellow option is the loop around Jordan Pond by the red-barn visitor center; the workout is the roughly six-mile High Ridge Loop, about 1,150 feet of climb across exposed grassland. Treat it like Briones: early starts in summer, plenty of water, and a foxtail check afterward. Bring cash for the kiosk.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 quiet, lightly trafficked alternative to the marquee parks for off-leash ridge hiking
  • 👍 High Ridge loop rewards the climb with sweeping South Bay views
  • 👍 voice-control off-leash allowed across most of the open space, with clear signage on which trails require leashes
  • ⚠️ grazing cattle roam the hillsides, so dogs need to be heeled or leashed around herds
  • ⚠️ upper hillside trails are fully exposed with sparse shade - rough on hot days
  • ⚠️ trails get muddy and storm-damaged after rain, and the small May Road lot fills fast on weekends

Recurring themes from owner reviews across Yelp, AllTrails, TripAdvisor, DogTrekker.

Mission Peak Regional Preserve (Fremont)

Address: Ohlone College entrance: 43600 Mission Blvd, Fremont; Stanford Avenue Staging Area at the east end of Stanford Avenue, Fremont · Fenced: No · Hours: Ohlone College entrance 6am–10pm daily; Stanford Avenue 6:30am–8pm or 9pm by season — strictly enforced

★ 4.7 · 4,513 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance6.2 mi round trip
Elevation gain~2,100 ft
DifficultyStrenuous
Off-leashNominal on paper; plan on leash
Leash ruleLeashed at staging, the first 200 ft, and around cattle
ShadeNone on the Stanford Ave route
WaterTap at the Stanford Ave trailhead; none on the climb
Parking / feeFree at Stanford Ave; Ohlone charges (about $4)

The famous grind to the 2,517-foot summit is 6.2 miles round trip with about 2,100 feet of gain — doable with a fit dog, but only in cool weather. The district's own page is blunt: several dogs die of heat stroke and dehydration here every year. Bring at least two liters of water for you and your dog, avoid midday in summer, and watch for heavy panting, dry gums, and weakness. There is essentially no shade on the Stanford Avenue route; in July and August, go at gate opening or pick Redwood instead.

Parking sets the day. The Stanford Avenue lot has just 43 spaces, fills before 7am on weekends, and sits inside a residential permit zone. The Ohlone College entrance has over 900 spaces and a longer, more gradual, partly shaded route to the top. Budget about five hours round trip, and don't linger past closing — hours are enforced with citations.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 panoramic summit views over the whole South Bay feel genuinely earned
  • 👍 off-leash allowed in the open space for fit, well-conditioned dogs
  • 👍 the Ohlone College start is longer but gentler and adds shaded forest, making it the smarter route with a dog
  • ⚠️ almost no shade on the main route and dogs have died of heatstroke here - reviewers insist on cool days, early starts, and lots of water
  • ⚠️ the tiny Stanford Avenue lot fills before 7am and overflow parking adds a long roadside walk
  • ⚠️ mid-day and weekend crowds are heavy enough to spoil the hike

Recurring themes from owner reviews across AllTrails, TripAdvisor, BringFido, DogTrekker.

Coyote Hills Regional Park (Fremont)

Address: 8000 Patterson Ranch Road, Fremont · Fenced: No · Hours: Gates roughly 7am–6pm winter to 8am–8pm summer; park curfew 10pm–5am

★ 4.7 · 3,385 Google reviews · on Google Maps

Distance~3.5 mi Bayview loop
Elevation gain~150 ft
DifficultyEasy
Off-leashUpland hill trails only
Leash ruleLeashed on paved Bayview; no dogs in the marsh or wetlands
ShadeAlmost none; exposed and windy
WaterTaps at the visitor center; bay and marsh off-limits
Parking / fee$5/vehicle

Coyote Hills packs 1,266 acres of bayshore hills and marsh into one of the South Bay's most scenic easy walks: the paved, roughly 3.5-mile Bayview loop circles the hills with open-water views the whole way, over only about 150 feet of climb. It is also the most restricted park here for dogs — district rules ban them from all wetlands and marshes, which closes the boardwalk and marsh trails, and the Bayview Trail itself is a posted leash path. Off-leash is limited to the unposted upland hill trails; for real off-leash room, drive up to Garin.

Two logistics: on busy weekends the park closes vehicle access once the lots fill (overflow at Dumbarton Quarry Campground), so arrive early. And if you continue into the adjacent Don Edwards San Francisco Bay National Wildlife Refuge, leashed dogs are allowed only on the Tidelands, Harrier Spur, and Quarry Trails and Marshlands Road — and nowhere else in the refuge.

Official page

What dog owners say:

  • 👍 flat, mostly paved Bayview loop is ideal for easy leashed walks, strollers, and senior dogs
  • 👍 wide-open bay and skyline views with abundant birdlife along the marshes
  • 👍 consistently clean, well-maintained facilities and picnic areas
  • ⚠️ leash-only park, and dogs are banned entirely from the marsh trails and adjacent wildlife refuge
  • ⚠️ almost no shade and the bay side gets seriously windy - conditions can flip fast
  • ⚠️ paid parking plus a per-dog fee at a cash-only machine annoys repeat visitors

Recurring themes from owner reviews across AllTrails, TripAdvisor, Hikes Dogs Love, Bark Park Finder.

Know Before You Go

  • The EBRPD off-leash rule, precisely: dogs may be off-leash in open space and undeveloped areas of parkland if they are under voice control at all times — in view, near you, and returning immediately when called. They must be leashed (six-foot maximum) in all developed areas: parking lots, picnic sites, lawns, campgrounds, paved multi-use trails, posted trails, and anywhere grazing animals are present.
  • The 200-foot rule: dogs must stay leashed within 200 feet of any parking lot, trailhead, or staging area — the district calls it a cooling-off period.
  • Where dogs are banned outright: all EBRPD swimming pools, swim beaches, wetlands, marshes, and designated nature study areas — including the entire Tilden Nature Area and the Huckleberry preserve trails next to Sibley.
  • Dog limit: a maximum of three dogs per person; more than three, or any paid dog walking, requires the district's annual dog-walker permit.
  • Carry a leash for every dog even where off-leash is allowed, and leash immediately if your dog shows any aggression. Failure to control a dog is a violation of EBRPD Ordinance 38.
  • Pack out poop bags: the district's rule is explicit — bag it and take it with you or bin it. Leaving bags beside the trail counts as littering.
  • Heat kills dogs here. EBRPD reports dogs dying of heat stroke and dehydration at Mission Peak every year. In summer, hike at dawn, choose shaded parks like Redwood, carry water for your dog, and never leave a dog in a parked car.
  • Rattlesnakes are active on East Bay trails roughly spring through fall. Keep your dog on the trail and out of tall grass and rock piles, and if a snake bites your dog, get to a veterinarian immediately.
  • Foxtails — the barbed dry grass seeds that blanket these hills from late spring through fall — burrow into paws, ears, and noses and often require a vet visit. Check your dog thoroughly after every grassland hike.
  • Water hazards: check blue-green algae advisories before letting dogs near any lake (Lake Chabot had a Danger advisory posted in July 2026), and never let dogs eat raw salmon or trout or drink from streams — the district warns both can be deadly.
  • Cattle and horses: many of these parks are actively grazed. Leash your dog around cattle and walk around herds; horses have right-of-way on all trails, so leash up and step aside as riders pass.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can my dog really hike off-leash in East Bay regional parks?

Yes — EBRPD is one of the few park agencies in the country that allows it. Dogs may be off-leash in undeveloped open-space areas as long as they are under genuine voice control, meaning in sight, close by, and returning the moment you call. You must still carry a six-foot leash per dog and use it in parking lots, picnic areas, posted trails, and around grazing animals.

Which East Bay parks and areas don't allow dogs at all?

The Tilden Nature Area (including Little Farm and Jewel Lake) is completely closed to dogs, as are the Huckleberry preserve trails adjacent to Sibley. District-wide, dogs are banned from all swim beaches, pools, wetlands, marshes, and designated nature-study areas — which is why the marsh side of Coyote Hills is off-limits. Most of the Don Edwards National Wildlife Refuge next to Coyote Hills is also closed to dogs.

How many dogs can I bring?

Up to three personal dogs per person. Walking more than three, or walking any dogs for pay, requires EBRPD's annual dog-walker permit, and even permit holders are limited to six dogs on an approved trail list.

Is Mission Peak safe for dogs in summer?

Not in the heat of the day. The district's own page says several dogs die there of heat stroke and dehydration every year — the route has essentially no shade or reliable water. If you go in summer, start at gate opening with at least two liters of water for the dog alone, watch for heavy panting and weakness, and turn around early. On genuinely hot days, choose shaded Redwood Regional Park instead.

Do these parks charge for dogs?

The official pages we checked list per-vehicle parking fees (typically $5 where charged) but no separate dog fee at these locations. Point Isabel, Tilden, Sibley, and Anthony Chabot have free parking; Briones and Garin take cash only at attended kiosks. Check the official page for current fees before you go.
